nodes.label: Shadow banking
nodes.rationale: Risiko yang muncul ketika disrupsi non-bank menggerus peran perbankan. Mitigasinya tidak cukup hanya dengan interkoneksi teknis. Hal 21 dan 35.

nodes.label: Urgensi penataan struktur industri dan manajemen risiko
nodes.norm_label: urgensi penataan struktur industri dan manajemen risiko
nodes.rationale: Peran non-bank menguat, tetapi interlink bank dengan non-bank belum memadai. Struktur industri yang terfragmentasi menambah kompleksitas pengendalian risiko dan pengawasan, sehingga risiko shadow banking masih menjadi isu. Hal 21-23.

nodes.label: Visi 3: Interlink bank-fintech
nodes.rationale: Disrupsi non-bank mendorong risiko shadow banking. Struktur industri yang konsolidatif menuntut kejelasan peran dan tanggung jawab antarpihak yang terafiliasi. Hal 35-36.

nodes.label: Konsolidasi struktur industri
nodes.rationale: Struktur industri yang konsolidatif dibutuhkan agar industri mampu mengendalikan risiko dan bersaing. Ditujukan untuk memitigasi shadow banking. Hal 2, 21, 41, dan 57.

nodes.label: Kesimpulan Penelitian
nodes.rationale: Tiga pilar WGM, EMA, dan Softmax Sharding diuji terhadap serangan Byzantine dan skalabilitas komunikasi.

nodes.label: Latency Jitter
nodes.rationale: Variabilitas latensi API memengaruhi keandalan SLA oracle.

nodes.label: Persentil ke-95
nodes.rationale: Sekitar 5 persen ronde baseline melebihi 7,5 menit sehingga p95 menjadi metrik SLA kritis.

nodes.label: Worst-Case Peak
nodes.rationale: Puncak latensi terburuk menentukan risiko timeout dan kegagalan transaksi oracle.

nodes.label: Dynamic Healing
nodes.rationale: EMA mendeteksi jarak ekstrem penyerang dan mendegradasi reputasinya, sehingga Λ kembali di atas batas kritis.

nodes.label: Faktor Smoothing EMA Lambda
nodes.rationale: Nilai lambda = 0,3.

nodes.label: Gerbang Penyaring Komite
nodes.rationale: Agen bereputasi rendah dikeluarkan secara disproporsional sebelum evaluasi dimulai.

nodes.label: Penalti Instan Stateful
nodes.rationale: Penalti absolut tanpa grace period mencabut hak suara penyerang sejak pengkhianatan pertama.

nodes.label: Reputasi Awal T0
nodes.rationale: Nilai T0 = 0,5.

nodes.label: Shock Absorber
nodes.rationale: Komite kecil mengurangi dominasi slow-responders pada ronde dan cenderung memilih evaluator bereputasi tinggi.

nodes.label: Softmax Sharding
nodes.rationale: Memilih subset evaluator berukuran tetap secara probabilistik untuk menurunkan kompleksitas komunikasi dari O(N^2) menjadi O(K^2).

nodes.label: Ukuran Komite K
nodes.rationale: Nilai K = 10.

nodes.label: Laju Partisipasi Jahat

nodes.label: Metodologi Komparasi Baseline

nodes.label: Min-Max Normalization
nodes.rationale: Rata-rata jarak diubah menjadi skor performa dengan batas terbalik, sehingga skor tinggi berarti kinerja baik.

nodes.label: Trade-off Akurasi dan Skalabilitas

nodes.label: Ilusi Ketahanan Pasif
nodes.rationale: Akurasi tinggi baseline pada noise acak dicapai lewat brute-force, sehingga margin Λ_c merosot seiring eskalasi f.

nodes.label: Passive Shadow Tracking

nodes.label: eNaira (Nigeria CBDC)
nodes.rationale: CBN motivations: financial inclusion, cheaper remittances, reduced informality (pdf p.6). Launched 25 October 2021 as Africa's first CBDC (pdf p.9). Built on Hyperledger Fabric (pdf p.10).

nodes.label: Auer and Boehme (2020), CBDC taxonomy
nodes.rationale: Source of the three-model CBDC taxonomy in Figure 1 (single-tier retail, indirect, intermediated) (pdf p.9).

nodes.label: Bank Verification Number (BVN)
nodes.rationale: Required for Tier 2 and Tier 3 wallets and for the merchant MD or CEO (Table 1).

nodes.label: BIS (2021), CBDC financial stability implications
nodes.rationale: Argues that even a benign CBDC launch lowers bank profitability through deposit and reserve losses (pdf p.29).

nodes.label: Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN)
nodes.rationale: Issuer of the eNaira, a liability of the CBN (pdf p.9). Launched a single-currency national CBDC (pdf p.21). All permissioned eNaira nodes are CBN computers (pdf p.11).

nodes.label: DCash (ECCU)
nodes.rationale: Cited as a CBDC with a months-long outage, so 24/7 eNaira operation cannot be taken for granted (fn 25).

nodes.label: Digital Currency Management System (DCMS)
nodes.rationale: Developed by Bitt Inc. Appendix 1 (pdf p.39) shows a Commerce Engine with KYC, MFA and audit services, a Numa component, a minting system with an HSM, and Hyperledger Fabric as the ledger.

nodes.label: BIS, CPMI, IMF and World Bank (2022), CBDCs for cross-border payments
nodes.norm_label: bis, cpmi, imf and world bank (2022), cbdcs for cross-border payments
nodes.rationale: Report to the G20 on two cross-border routes: foreign access to a domestic CBDC, or multi-CBDC arrangements (fn 44).

nodes.label: GIABA Mutual Evaluation Report (2021)
nodes.rationale: Identified AML/CFT deficiencies in Nigeria that remain to be addressed (pdf p.30).

nodes.label: GSMA (2020), Many Paths to Mobile Money Interoperability
nodes.norm_label: gsma (2020), many paths to mobile money interoperability
nodes.rationale: Bilateral interoperability is one of the three most common models (fn 42).

nodes.label: Hyperledger Fabric
nodes.rationale: Underlying transaction network and ledger of the eNaira (pdf p.10). Described as a permissioned DLT (fn 19). Paper cites its release 2.5 documentation (fn 16).

nodes.label: Hyperledger Fabric documentation, release 2.5
nodes.rationale: Cited for the transaction flow (txflow) documentation of Fabric release 2.5 (fn 16).

nodes.label: IMF (2018), Casting Light on Central Bank Digital Currencies
nodes.norm_label: imf (2018), casting light on central bank digital currencies
nodes.rationale: Argues CBDC user appeal is limited in advanced economies but may be greater where banking penetration is low (fn 27).

nodes.label: IMF (2020), Digital Money Across Borders
nodes.rationale: Says peer-to-peer CBDC transfers flatten correspondent banking, shorten payment chains and cut transaction time (fn 50).

nodes.label: IMF Nigeria Article IV Consultation Staff Reports (2020 to 2022)
nodes.norm_label: imf nigeria article iv consultation staff reports (2020 to 2022)
nodes.rationale: Cited for remittance and balance-of-payments pressures (pdf p.7), the parallel market (pdf p.27) and AML/CFT deficiencies (pdf p.30).

nodes.label: Nigeria’s eNaira, One Year After (IMF Working Paper WP/23/104)
nodes.norm_label: nigeria’s enaira, one year after (imf working paper wp/23/104)
nodes.rationale: Cover shows May 2022. Copyright page (pdf p.2) and recommended citation give 2023. Cite 2023 and flag the mismatch.

nodes.label: International money transfer operators (IMTOs)
nodes.rationale: Named examples: MoneyGram and Western Union. Charge 7.8 to 8.7 percent per transaction (pdf p.6).

nodes.label: Katz and Shapiro (1985), network externalities
nodes.rationale: Defines network externality as utility that rises with the number of other users of a good (fn 62).

nodes.label: Liebowitz and Margolis (1994), network externality survey
nodes.norm_label: liebowitz and margolis (1994), network externality survey
nodes.rationale: Cited as a concise survey of the network externality literature (fn 63).

nodes.label: Mobile money providers (MMPs)
nodes.rationale: Run cash-in cash-out agent networks (pdf p.18). May onboard clients to eNaira (fn 35). Telcos cannot lead mobile money services in Nigeria (fn 33).

nodes.label: National Identification Number (NIN)
nodes.rationale: Tier 1 requires a verified national ID number (Table 1). Phase 2 opens wallets for unbanked people with a NIN (pdf p.15).

nodes.label: Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation (NDIC)
nodes.rationale: Insures mobile money deposits up to N500,000 through a pass-through arrangement (fn 40). Requires MMPs to hold fidelity bond insurance (fn 39).

nodes.label: NIBSS (central switch for mobile money)
nodes.rationale: Mobile money regulation requires MMPs to connect to this central switch for interoperability (fn 42).

nodes.label: DCMS Numa (queues and submits transactions)
nodes.rationale: Queues transactions and submits them to Hyperledger Fabric for real-time settlement (pdf p.10).

nodes.label: World Bank Remittance Prices Worldwide database
nodes.norm_label: world bank remittance prices worldwide database
nodes.rationale: Cost of sending 200 dollars in cash to Nigeria was 10.4 percent in 2020Q2, of which 4.8 points were FX spread (fn 49).

nodes.label: Sand Dollar (Bahamas CBDC)
nodes.rationale: Bahamas launched a fully public CBDC before Nigeria (pdf p.6). Its governor named merchant network, interoperability, bank participation and user education as key lessons (fn 2).

nodes.label: Account-based ledger
nodes.rationale: Makes transactions traceable to identified individuals (pdf p.11). The paper calls this design largely appropriate for AML/CFT risks (pdf p.30).

nodes.label: AML/CFT risks of CBDC
nodes.rationale: A cashless economy may reduce AML/CFT risk, but anonymity and digital form bring new risks (pdf p.30). The existing framework may not fully address them (pdf p.11).

nodes.label: Byzantine fault tolerance (BFT)
nodes.rationale: Integrity holds while most nodes are honest (fn 18). CBN asks whether Fabric's BFT-style block validation and supermajority threshold apply to the eNaira (Appendix 2, pdf p.41 and p.43).

nodes.label: Cashless trend
nodes.rationale: Mobile phones and electronic payments make some economies effectively cashless. The trend may worsen inequality for people without access to electronic payment (Box 1, pdf p.8).

nodes.label: Central bank digital currency (CBDC)
nodes.rationale: Framed as a digital fiat currency that fits the cashless trend and fills the financial inclusion vacuum (pdf p.8). Network effects mean adoption needs a coordinated policy push (pdf p.2).

nodes.label: Cash-in cash-out (CICO) agent network
nodes.rationale: Mobile phone agents give mobile money a universal presence (pdf p.18). The eNaira could use this distribution network (pdf p.18, p.21).

nodes.label: Complementary relationship with mobile money
nodes.rationale: CBN stays out of retail services and supplies CBDC to market players as a bridge. CBDC wallets lack payment tracking, so mobile money stays the main account (pdf p.18 to p.19).

nodes.label: Correspondent banking chain
nodes.rationale: Cross-border remittance runs through wire transfers and nostro accounts across two domestic systems. Each layer adds cost and time (pdf p.23; Box 3 on pdf p.25).

nodes.label: Currency substitution and capital flow volatility
nodes.norm_label: currency substitution and capital flow volatility
nodes.rationale: Wider CBDC adoption abroad, or domestic use of global stablecoins, could cause currency substitution and capital flow volatility (pdf p.29, fn 55).

nodes.label: Deposit disintermediation and bank funding risk
nodes.norm_label: deposit disintermediation and bank funding risk
nodes.rationale: CBDC may crowd out bank intermediation and raise run risk (pdf p.28 to p.29). CBN's choice not to pay interest on eNaira and its tiered ceilings are treated as adequate safeguards (pdf p.29).

nodes.label: Direct access for foreign IMTOs
nodes.rationale: CBN's preferred remittance option: foreign IMTOs own eNaira merchant wallets (pdf p.22, fn 48). Needs home-host AML/CFT arrangements (fn 45).

nodes.label: Distributed ledger technology (DLT)
nodes.rationale: Advantages: resistance to hacking and no single point of failure. Limitation: slower processing and block sealing at the expected transaction volumes (pdf p.11).

nodes.label: eNaira phase 2 expansion
nodes.rationale: Extends coverage to people without bank accounts (NIN-based wallets, cash-in agents) and to people without internet (USSD). Phase 1 was limited to bank account holders (pdf p.6, p.14).

nodes.label: Financial inclusion
nodes.rationale: 38 million Nigerians (36 percent of adults) lack bank accounts. From August 2022 eNaira wallets were open to phone users without bank accounts (pdf p.6).

nodes.label: FX spread (exchange rate margin)
nodes.rationale: Accounts for about half of Nigeria's remittance cost (pdf p.24). eNaira does not remove the need for currency conversion at the border (pdf p.23).

nodes.label: Indirect CBDC (ICBDC)
nodes.rationale: CBDC is issued only to banks, which then issue indirect CBDC to their clients (pdf p.9).

nodes.label: Informal economy
nodes.rationale: Informal transactions and employment equal over half of GDP and 80 percent of employment. An account-based eNaira may make informal payments traceable and widen the tax base (pdf p.6).

nodes.label: Intermediated (two-tier) CBDC
nodes.rationale: Central bank issues CBDC to banks against reserve deposits, and banks handle retail transactions with nonbank PSPs (pdf p.9 to p.10). The eNaira's retail end may be seen as this model (pdf p.9).

nodes.label: Low adoption of eNaira in year one
nodes.norm_label: low adoption of enaira in year one
nodes.rationale: About 860,000 retail wallets, 0.8 percent of active bank accounts. About 14,000 transactions a week, or 1.5 percent of wallets (pdf p.13 to p.14). The text dates the wallet count to end-November 2021, but Figure 2 runs to November 2022.

nodes.label: Multi-CBDC (mCBDC) arrangements
nodes.rationale: A multi-currency CBDC platform could allow direct CBDC-to-CBDC interoperability without correspondent banks (pdf p.31). The paper calls this a more game-changing cost saving. The DCMS may support it (fn 60).

nodes.label: Merchant adoption of eNaira
nodes.rationale: Merchants need integrated benefits (lower fees, cheaper cash handling, security) to add to consumer take-up (pdf p.28). Merchant balances convert to the linked bank account at day end (fn 23, pdf p.11).

nodes.label: Mobile money interoperability
nodes.rationale: Bilateral transfers between MMPs need costly, data-intensive and risky clearing and settlement (fn 42, pdf p.21). eNaira wallets could cut those costs (pdf p.21).

nodes.label: Network externality (network effect)
nodes.rationale: The value of eNaira rises with the number of users, so breaking the low-adoption equilibrium needs clever strategy and luck (pdf p.14). Annex II models it (pdf p.35).

nodes.label: Parallel market spread
nodes.rationale: Reached 60 percent by end-2022. Since December 2020 CBN requires remittances in the currency of origin, so eNaira would bring back currency conversion (pdf p.27).

nodes.label: Permissioned distributed ledger technology
nodes.rationale: Node permissions can be customized (fn 19). All eNaira nodes are CBN computers, which makes the setup close to a centrally managed distributed database (fn 20).

nodes.label: Programmable payments
nodes.rationale: Programmable CBDC payments can give instant rebates or transfers to customers and suppliers, for example to shift electricity use (pdf p.28).

nodes.label: Remittance
nodes.rationale: Remittance receipts were 24 billion dollars in 2019, or 5.3 percent of GDP (pdf p.6). The government sought to cut transfer costs with frictionless digital money.

nodes.label: Single-tier retail CBDC
nodes.rationale: Central bank onboards retail clients directly and handles all retail payments (Figure 1, pdf p.9).

nodes.label: Social cash transfer programs
nodes.rationale: Government transfers into eNaira wallets remove most distribution cost and embezzlement risk. Recipients keep risk-free money (pdf p.28).

nodes.label: Stablecoins
nodes.rationale: The collapse of Terra showed the danger of unregulated stablecoins. Retail CBDCs could serve as stablecoin substitutes (Box 1, pdf p.8).

nodes.label: Substitutive relationship with mobile money
nodes.rationale: CBN would act as the direct retail provider. The paper warns of industry reshuffle, governance risk and governments picking winners. A private-public partnership over APIs is the alternative (pdf p.21).

nodes.label: Tiered KYC framework
nodes.rationale: CBN's three-tier KYC circular (fn 22). It has been the prevailing AML/CFT backbone in Nigeria since 2013 (pdf p.11). Identity evidence rises with each tier (pdf p.12).

nodes.label: Tiered wallet system
nodes.rationale: Tier 0 needs only a phone number. Tier 1 adds a verified national ID number. Tiers 2 and 3 use BVN, and Tier 3 requires full KYC under CBN's 2009 AML/CFT regulation. Limits rise with each tier (Table 1, pdf p.12).

nodes.label: Tipping point and high and low adoption equilibria
nodes.norm_label: tipping point and high and low adoption equilibria
nodes.rationale: The starting point decides whether adoption ends in a low or a high equilibrium. A mass campaign must push adoption past the tipping point (Box 2, pdf p.16).

nodes.label: Transaction and balance ceilings
nodes.rationale: Limit deposit disintermediation and AML/CFT risk (pdf p.11). Also limit substitution of mobile money by CBDC (pdf p.19). The DCMS can set dynamic limits per wallet type (pdf p.29).
